title: Forty-one ritual directions out of one temple, and a shrine count nobody agrees on
register: documentary, and the count itself is disputed
summary: A social group was bound to a particular spring, stone or hill outside Cusco, and owed it offerings in a fixed order radiating from the Temple of the Sun; the debt, not a road, was the connection. Colonial investigators trying to abolish the system produced the only inventory that survives of it, and even that inventory cannot agree with itself on whether there were 41 lines or 42, 328 shrines or 340 or 450. What ended for certain was the imperial authority that ranked the lines and fed the shrines; what did not end were the springs, the stones, and the debts people still owed them under other names.

nodes.name: Coricancha
nodes.note: The conceptual origin of the ceque ordering and the state's principal solar temple, where the four suyus met. Its precinct and fine masonry were occupied by the Dominicans after 1533 and a monastery built over the Inca fabric.

nodes.name: Huanacauri
nodes.note: A mountain southeast of Cusco and, with the Coricancha, one of the two most important places in Cobo's account. Embedded in Inca origin tradition and the Warachikoy initiation of noble youths; Killke and Inca material at nearby sites supports long use.

nodes.name: Matagua
nodes.note: Where initiates slept below Huanacauri before the sunrise ascent and left their sacrificial llamas. Molina describes the rite; the identification with the modern Matao locality is Bauer's proposal, not a certainty.

nodes.name: Tambomachay
nodes.note: An Inca lodging used for hunting, named on the Antisuyu's first ceque alongside springs called Tipcpuquiu and Quinoapuquiu. Its monumental fountains survive; matching every recorded spring to a surviving feature remains partly reconstructive.

nodes.name: Sacsahuaman
nodes.note: A fortress and ceremonial complex venerated as a whole and in its parts; Cobo's list attaches several surrounding rocks, fountains and a stone seat to different ceques rather than treating it as a single node.

nodes.name: Guaracince
nodes.modern: Chuquipampa, within the Coricancha precinct, Cusco
nodes.note: A level area within the Sun Temple complex, Ch. 2:1, considered the place from which earthquakes originated. Offerings reportedly included children, sacrificed camelids, burned clothing and buried gold and silver during earthquakes.

nodes.name: Michosamaro
nodes.note: Ch. 1:1, a place near the Totocache slope where tradition held that a companion of Manco Capac was turned to stone. Offerings of gold, clothing and marine shell were made to obtain good rain.

nodes.name: Pilcopuquio
nodes.note: Ch. 1:3, a fountain and source of an irrigation ditch. Its place in the ordered list is direct evidence that the network's cult, water management and royal memory overlapped in a single node.

nodes.name: Cirocaya
nodes.note: Ch. 1:4, a cave believed to release hail. Collective sacrifice at this node sought to prevent crop damage.

nodes.name: Vilcacona
nodes.note: An. 2:1, a ceremonial gathering node where portable huacas and idols from across Cusco were reportedly assembled, sacrificed to together on a fixed occasion, and returned to their places: a temporary aggregation hub for sacred objects.

nodes.name: Curovilca
nodes.note: An. 2:4, a quarry where sacrifice sought both continued stone supply and the structural stability of buildings made from it, linking extraction, construction and ritual risk.

nodes.name: Chuquimarca
nodes.modern: Mantocalla hill, Antisuyu sector, Cusco vicinity
nodes.note: An. 3:4, a temple of the Sun on Mantocalla hill where the Sun was said to descend and sleep. Cobo reports child sacrifice among its offerings.

nodes.name: Chuquicancha
nodes.note: An. 6:3, a hill regarded as a house of the Sun. Molina associates it with sacrifices to the Sun, Thunder and Moon and prayers for the ruler's health, prosperity and victory.

nodes.name: Cachicalla
nodes.note: A wayside shrine where passers-by reportedly offered coca taken directly from their own mouths, an unusually cheap and continuous form of the system's differential offerings.

nodes.name: Anta
nodes.note: A point on the Chinchaysuyu route along which runners carried ritual affliction outward from Cusco during Citua, to be relayed onward toward Tilca and the Apurímac.

nodes.name: Apurímac River
nodes.note: The terminal deposit for purificatory material carried out of Cusco on the Chinchaysuyu route during Citua: the ceremony transferred danger from the imperial center to flowing water.

nodes.name: Huillque pass
nodes.note: Near Quiachilli, the terminus of the longest reconstructed ceque sequence, at least forty-five kilometers from the Coricancha before it continues to several unidentified nodes.

nodes.name: Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui
nodes.note: Colonial tradition credits him with rebuilding Cusco, monumentalizing the Coricancha and reorganizing its shrines; at least nineteen recorded huacas are tied to him. Rowe treated him as the system's principal architect; Bauer treats this as the largest single contribution to a cumulative process, not a one-act design.

nodes.name: The Sapa Inca and court
nodes.note: The office, not any one ruler: founded and monumentalized temples, designated or relocated huacas, assigned sacrifices, and used shrines for coronation, warfare, hunting and dynastic legitimation. Continuous across Pachacuti, Topa Inca, Huayna Capac and their successors until the Spanish occupation of Cusco.

nodes.name: The royal panacas
nodes.note: Cusco's royal descent groups, maintaining the cults of deceased rulers. The conservative reconstruction assigns one ceque to each of ten panacas, five in Hurin Cusco and five in Hanan Cusco, though Cobo does not name every responsible group consistently.

nodes.name: The nonroyal ayllus
nodes.note: Ten nonroyal descent groups integrated into Cusco's social order, named in Cobo as Goacaytaqui, Vicaquirao, Usca Mayta and others, supplying attendants, maintaining shrines and presenting offerings. The custodians of nearly half the recorded ceques remain unknown.

nodes.name: The huacacamayocs
nodes.note: The shrine custodians and specialists: they knew a huaca's name, origin account, required offering, correct occasion, prayers and responsible group. This expertise made them the specific targets of Polo's and Albornoz's investigations.

nodes.name: Capacocha
nodes.note: The irregular, empire-spanning state ceremony in which children and valuable offerings were dedicated and carried from or through Cusco to provincial huacas, sometimes cutting directly across the landscape rather than following the royal roads. A documented land dispute shows carriers invoking a capacocha's endpoint to extend a territorial claim.

nodes.name: Juan Polo de Ondegardo
nodes.note: Corregidor of Cusco, December 1558 to December 1560 and again 1571–1572. Investigated Inca institutions using indigenous specialists and produced a chart or account of the ceques that Bauer thinks is the lost source Cobo later copied, though Rowe left the authorship open.

nodes.name: Cristóbal de Molina
nodes.note: Priest and Quechua speaker who interviewed elderly former participants for Bishop Lartaún and wrote the fullest surviving procedural account of Warachikoy, Citua, Inti Raymi, Capac Raymi and capacocha. His separate huaca list is lost.

nodes.name: Cristóbal de Albornoz
nodes.note: Ecclesiastical visitor and extirpator who campaigned against Taqui Onqoy and huaca worship, compiled an independent Chinchaysuyu shrine list around 1582, and claimed to have destroyed more than two thousand huacas in the Chanca and Aymara areas.

nodes.name: Bernabé Cobo
nodes.note: Jesuit chronicler who completed Historia del Nuevo Mundo in 1653, preserving the fullest ordered list of ceques and huacas by copying an earlier, now-lost manuscript. His stated purpose was to demonstrate what he saw as indigenous credulity, and his abbreviation and spelling introduce their own distortions.

nodes.name: The Coricancha's gold and silver
nodes.note: The precious-metal decoration of the state cult's central temple, especially vulnerable to seizure and melting once Spanish forces occupied Cusco in 1533.

nodes.name: The lost ceque manuscript
nodes.note: The original chart or account of Cusco's ceques and huacas, probably compiled around 1559 and possibly by Polo de Ondegardo, now lost. It survives only through Cobo's 1653 copy, itself abbreviated and corrupted in transmission.
